hub.description: Decks and fences for Hendersonville, TN homes, from raised decks on Old Hickory Lake lots to privacy fences in newer HOA subdivisions.
hub.intro: Plenty of Hendersonville backyards slope down toward Old Hickory Lake, and that slope shapes a lot of deck and fence plans in town. On the lake side, the back of the house often sits a full story above the yard, so a deck there stands on tall posts. A fence has a different problem, because it needs to give you privacy without hiding the water. Homes away from the shoreline have their own concerns, mostly HOA rules and graded yards in newer subdivisions. For more detail on Hendersonville projects, see our [Hendersonville deck builder page](/deck-builder-hendersonville-tn/) or our page on [fence installation in Hendersonville](/fence-company-hendersonville-tn/).

sections.heading: Lake lots and the view you want to keep
paragraphs: If your Hendersonville house backs up to the lake, the view is likely a big part of why you bought it. A new deck should get you closer to that view, and a new fence should not take it away. So on a lake lot, plan the two together. The deck usually comes off the main floor, high above a yard that falls away toward the water. Fencing tends to work best in two parts: solid panels along the side lines near the house, then something lower or more open as the line runs toward the lake.

Wind and sun belong in the plan too. Open water gives wind a long run at the back of the house, and a tall solid fence or a raised deck takes the brunt of it. Depending on which way the lot faces, a lake deck in Hendersonville may sit in full sun most of the afternoon. None of that rules anything out. It just changes which materials make sense and how the posts get set.

sections.heading: Where your lot ends and Corps land begins
paragraphs: Old Hickory Lake is managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. On many lake lots in Hendersonville, the strip of ground along the shoreline is Corps property and not part of the homeowner's lot. People are often surprised by that. Anything built on that strip, or at the water's edge, needs approval from the Corps under its own shoreline rules. That process is separate from the city, and a city permit does not cover it. Before anyone draws a deck or a fence line on a lake lot, find your survey or plat and see where your line really runs.

On your side of that line, the rules come from different places. Inside Hendersonville city limits, the city codes office reviews building permits. Some homes with a Hendersonville mailing address actually sit in unincorporated Sumner County, and the county handles those. If you have an HOA, its review comes on top of either one. Requirements vary, so confirm with the right office before you settle on a design.

sections.heading: Digging footings and posts in Hendersonville
paragraphs: Dig in much of Hendersonville and you usually go through clay first, and you may hit limestone not far below. Neither has to be a problem when the plan expects it. Clay holds water after a rain and shrinks as it dries, so deck footings and fence posts need enough depth and good drainage. Rock can stop an auger before a hole is deep enough. When that happens, the layout may shift or the rock may need a heavier bit. It is better to talk about that at the estimate than to find out on build day.

Slope adds another layer. When a yard falls toward the lake or a creek, posts on the low side run much longer than the ones near the house, and a tall deck frame needs bracing so it stays stiff. Rain also runs downhill and collects at the low end of a deck or fence line. Planning for that water early keeps posts out of soggy ground and keeps soil from washing out around them.

sections.heading: Newer subdivisions and HOA review
paragraphs: Hendersonville has added a lot of new homes over the years, and many of them are in subdivisions with an HOA. If yours is one, expect the architectural committee to review a deck or fence before work starts. Their rules often cover fence height and style, and some reach as far as deck stain color. Get the covenants and the submission form early, because approval can take a while. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) covers what to include.

Newer Hendersonville yards have their own quirks. Builders often grade the lot and bring in fill, so the top layer near the house may be looser than it looks. Deck footings need to reach firm soil below any fill. Sod laid over packed subsoil can drain slowly, which leaves wet spots along the back of the house. Wherever your home is, from Walton Ferry to Bluegrass, walk the yard after a hard rain before deciding where posts go.

sections.heading: Planning a deck and a fence at the same time
paragraphs: Plenty of Hendersonville homeowners want both, a deck off the back and a fence to keep the dog in or the neighbors out. Planning them together helps. The fence can meet the deck at a sensible spot, and the gate can go where you actually walk from the stairs to the yard. With an HOA, you may be able to send both in one submission. If you only need one now, decide where the other would go later so the first does not box you in.

faqs.q: Does the Corps of Engineers need to approve a deck on my Old Hickory Lake lot?
faqs.a: Usually only when part of the project sits on Corps land or reaches the shoreline. A deck built entirely inside your own property line goes through the City of Hendersonville, or Sumner County if you are outside city limits, like any other deck. Anything that crosses onto Corps property, such as steps or a path down to the water, needs Corps approval first. Read your survey, plat and deed, since they show where your line runs and whether any easements affect the lake side.

faqs.q: Should the deck or the fence go in first?
faqs.a: In most cases the deck goes first. Digging footings and moving lumber is easier with the yard open, and the finished deck shows you where you will be looking out from. On a Hendersonville lake lot, that view tells you where the fence should switch to a lower or open style. If you need a fence right away for a dog, it can go in first with a gate or gap left wide enough for the deck work later.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my home is inside Hendersonville city limits?
faqs.a: A Hendersonville mailing address does not settle it on its own. The Sumner County property records for your parcel often show it, or you can call the city codes office with your address and ask. That answer decides which office reviews your deck or fence permit and which rules apply. It is worth checking before you draw up plans, especially near the edges of town where city and county land sit close together.

deck.description: Deck builder in Hendersonville, TN for raised decks on Old Hickory Lake lots, sloped yards, and newer HOA homes, with footings and permits explained.
deck.intro: Many deck projects in Hendersonville begin with a back door that sits well above the yard. On lots that fall toward Old Hickory Lake, the main floor often sits a full story up, sometimes over a walkout basement. A deck there has to stand steady on tall posts and still leave you a clear look at the water. Homes on flatter lots in newer subdivisions face a different hurdle, which is usually HOA approval. In both cases, a good deck builder should talk through the slope and the permits before anyone picks out boards.

sections.heading: Raised decks on Hendersonville lake lots
paragraphs: A deck on a Hendersonville lake lot is often a second story deck. The frame stands on long posts, and those posts need bracing so the deck does not sway when a group is out there. Stairs belong in the design from the start. On a steep yard they may need a landing partway down, and the bottom step should land on ground that will not wash out or turn to mud after a storm.

Plan the space under a raised deck early too. Some people want it dry enough to use as a shaded patio, which usually means adding a drainage system under the joists. Others would rather close it off with skirting to keep animals out. Each choice changes how the framing and the ground below get handled, so it is easier to decide before the posts go in.

sections.heading: Railings that keep the lake in view
paragraphs: Once a deck is well off the ground, code requires a railing, and when you sit down, the top rail sits close to eye level. Wide wood balusters can chop up the view you built the deck for. Thin metal balusters or cable railing let more of the lake through, though the Hendersonville codes office, or the county outside city limits, decides which styles pass inspection. A flat rail cap on top gives you a place to set a drink without adding bulk. Judge railing options from inside the house as well, since you will probably see the deck from indoors far more often than from the yard.

sections.heading: Footings in Hendersonville clay and rock
paragraphs: Nobody sees the footings once a deck is finished, but every post rests on one. Across much of Hendersonville, a hole goes through clay and then, fairly often, runs into limestone. Clay stays wet after heavy rain and shrinks as it dries. Each footing needs to sit below the frost line on firm, undisturbed soil. Local code sets the minimum depth, and in many places an inspector looks at the holes before concrete goes in.

Rock changes the plan rather than stopping it. A footing that reaches solid limestone before full depth may be able to bear on the rock, depending on what the inspector allows. Other times the hole moves over or the rock gets drilled. On a slope, shifting the footing layout a little can shorten the downhill posts. Ask any Hendersonville deck builder you talk to how they handle rock before you sign anything.

sections.heading: Boards for sun and shade near the lake
paragraphs: Lake decks in Hendersonville can sit in hard afternoon sun on one lot and deep shade under old trees on the next. That difference should drive the material choice. Composite boards skip the staining and resist rot, but they get hot underfoot in full summer sun, and dark colors get hotter. Pressure treated pine costs less up front and stays cooler to the touch, yet it needs regular cleaning and sealing. Shaded decks near the water tend to grow mildew on any material. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) goes through the tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Permits for a deck in Hendersonville
paragraphs: Most decks that attach to the house or sit well above grade need a building permit. Inside Hendersonville city limits, that runs through the city codes office. Homes in unincorporated Sumner County go through the county instead. Permit drawings usually show the footing layout and how the deck ties into the house, and inspections happen at set points during the build. Rules and steps vary, so confirm with the right office before you plan around a date. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process.

Two other reviews can apply on top of the permit. When stairs or a walkway reach onto Corps land near Old Hickory Lake, the Corps has to approve that part separately, and the city permit does not cover that ground. If your Hendersonville home is in an HOA, the architectural committee will usually want plans before work starts. It is smart to have both answers in hand before the permit application goes in.

sections.heading: Decks for newer Hendersonville homes
paragraphs: Newer houses around Hendersonville often come with a small builder landing or a bare patio slab out back. The yard was graded during construction, and the soil near the foundation may include fill that settles over time. Footings have to pass through that fill to firm ground, which can mean deeper holes than you would guess. Newer neighborhoods also tend to have an HOA with rules on deck placement and stain color. In Indian Lake, Sanders Ferry or any other part of town, the first steps are the same: pull your plat and read your covenants.

faqs.q: Can my deck stairs run all the way down to the lake?
faqs.a: Only as far as your property line, unless the Corps approves more. On many Old Hickory Lake lots in Hendersonville, the ground nearest the water is Corps property, and building there needs the Corps to sign off first, if it is allowed at all. A simple approach is to end the stairs at your line and handle any path beyond it through the Corps. Check your survey before the stair layout is set.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace my deck in Hendersonville?
faqs.a: Usually, when the frame or footings are being rebuilt. Swapping deck boards on a sound frame may be treated differently. The Hendersonville codes office, or Sumner County if you are outside city limits, can tell you what applies at your address. A replacement is also the time to check how the old deck was fastened to the house, since that ledger connection is a common failure point on older decks.

faqs.q: Will a raised deck darken my walkout basement?
faqs.a: On a sloped Hendersonville lot with a walkout lower level, it can. A raised deck shades the lower patio and cuts some daylight to the rooms behind it. Some owners like that shade in summer. If you would rather keep the light, the deck can be narrower where it passes the lower windows, or shifted to one side. Stand on the lower level with the plan in hand before the footings are marked.

faqs.q: How do you build a deck on a steep Hendersonville backyard?
faqs.a: The low side gets longer posts, and bracing keeps the frame stiff. Footings get placed to suit the slope rather than forced into a neat grid. Stairs often need a landing partway down. Rain runoff matters too, because a steep yard sends water straight toward the lowest footings. On the steepest lots, a deck that steps down in two levels can be easier to build and nicer to use than one tall platform.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before a deck builder visits?
faqs.a: Your survey or plat helps most, along with your HOA covenants if you have them. A rough idea of size and where you want the stairs to land is useful too. Photos taken from inside the house of the view you want to keep can guide railing choices. On any Hendersonville lot near the water, mark where you believe the back property line sits so it can be checked early. Then send the details through the [estimate form](#estimate).

fence.description: Fence installation in Hendersonville, TN for lake lots, sloped yards, and HOA subdivisions, with privacy fence options and tips for rocky post holes.
fence.intro: Fencing a Hendersonville yard often means balancing two things that pull against each other. You want privacy from the house next door, and if you live near Old Hickory Lake you also want to keep the water in sight. A dog brings its own needs, and so does a steep yard or an HOA with rules on fence style. Here is what a fence company should work out with you before the first post goes in.

sections.heading: Privacy and a lake view on one Hendersonville lot
paragraphs: On a Hendersonville lake lot, one common answer is to split the fence by job. A privacy fence runs along the side lines close to the house, where it blocks the view into the neighbor's patio. Closer to the water, the line changes to something lower or open, like metal pickets or a short wood style, so you can still see the lake from the deck and the windows. Make the switch at a post so the change looks planned instead of patched.

Your HOA may treat lake lots differently, so read the covenants before you choose a style. The fence also has to stop at your line. On many lake lots, the private lot ends short of the shoreline, and the strip past it is federal land that the Corps manages. A fence that wanders onto that strip can mean a request to take it down.

sections.heading: Start with the property line
paragraphs: Every sound fence installation in Hendersonville starts with knowing exactly where the lot ends. A recent survey or pinned corners are the reliable way to know. Building on a guess can put the fence on the neighbor's side, and moving it later usually costs more than the survey would have. Talk with the neighbors before the posts go in, too. Call Tennessee 811 before any digging so buried utility lines get marked. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) walks through the steps.

sections.heading: Setting fence posts in Hendersonville clay and rock
paragraphs: Posts are where a fence usually fails first when the ground is not handled right. Much of Hendersonville has clay soil, which holds water around the base of a post long after a storm. A layer of gravel under the concrete helps that water drain away instead of sitting against the wood. Shaping the top of the concrete so rain sheds off also helps a post last.

Then there is the rock. Limestone sits close to the surface in many parts of the area, and an auger can hit it well before a hole reaches full depth. At that point the usual options are drilling into the rock or shifting the post a little and adjusting the panel spacing to match. A post set shallow because the digging got hard will lean before long, and the rest of the line follows it.

sections.heading: Fencing a sloped yard with a dog
paragraphs: Plenty of Hendersonville yards drop toward the lake or a creek, which makes fence layout harder. With a racked fence, the panels follow the ground in a smooth line. A stepped fence keeps each panel level and drops it at every post, which leaves triangle shaped gaps along the bottom. Dogs that dig or squeeze can find those gaps fast, so they need a trimmed bottom board or a kickboard to close them. Gates on a slope also need care, since a gate hung without the grade in mind can drag. Our guide on [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) goes deeper.

sections.heading: HOA review for fences in Hendersonville subdivisions
paragraphs: Whether you live in Walton Ferry or Bluegrass, find out if your subdivision has covenants that cover fences. Many Hendersonville associations do. Height and style come up most often. Some also care which side faces out or what color the wood is stained, and some limit fences on corner lots or in front of the house. Get approval in writing before fence installation begins. Taking down a fence the committee never approved costs far more than the wait.

City rules apply alongside the HOA. Inside city limits, fence permits come from the Hendersonville Planning Department, which can tell you what applies near streets and on corner lots. Outside the city, check with Sumner County. A privacy fence that suits the HOA can still run into the city's rules for the street side of a corner lot, so ask both before you order materials.

sections.heading: Wind and weather near the water
paragraphs: Wind crossing the lake has little to slow it before it reaches a lakeside yard, and a solid privacy fence takes the full push. On an exposed Hendersonville lot, that can call for heavier posts set to full depth and stout gate hardware. Some owners pick a style with small gaps between boards so some of the wind can pass through. Wood close to the water may also stay damp longer, so seal it and keep mulch and soil from piling against the bottom boards. If a deck is also on your list, our page for [deck builders in Hendersonville](/deck-builder-hendersonville-tn/) covers that side of the yard.

faqs.q: Can I put a fence on the Corps land behind my lake lot?
faqs.a: Not without approval from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and you should not count on getting it. The Corps manages the shoreline of Old Hickory Lake under its own rules, separate from the City of Hendersonville. Your fence should stop at your surveyed property line. If you want anything past that line, talk to the Corps first and plan around their answer.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a fence in Hendersonville?
faqs.a: It depends on your address. Inside city limits, the city asks for a fence permit from the Hendersonville Planning Department before work starts, and that office can explain the rules on height and placement. Outside city limits, ask Sumner County. Pool fences and corner lots often carry extra rules. If you have an HOA, its approval is a separate step on top of anything the city or county requires.

faqs.q: What fence keeps my view of Old Hickory Lake?
faqs.a: Anything you can see through. Metal picket fence is a common pick on the lake side because the pickets are thin and spaced apart. A low wood fence or split rail also keeps sight lines open, although split rail alone will not hold a small dog. If you need privacy too, keep the solid sections close to the house, where they block the most.

faqs.q: How do I keep my dog in on a lake lot without losing the view?
faqs.a: Start with an open style that is still tight at the bottom. Metal picket with narrow spacing works for many dogs. Split rail with welded wire mesh on the inside is another option that keeps the look light. On a sloped yard, check the bottom gaps along every section. Gates should close and latch on their own, since a gate left open on a lake lot can mean a dog headed for the water.

faqs.q: Which side of a privacy fence should face the neighbor?
faqs.a: Many HOAs, and some local rules, call for the finished side to face out toward the neighbor or the street. Posts and rails then sit on your side. Even where it is not required, many owners do it as a courtesy. Board on board and shadowbox styles look finished from both sides, which sidesteps the question. Check your covenants before you choose, especially in newer Hendersonville subdivisions where the rules can be detailed. When you are ready, send your plans through the [estimate form](#estimate).
